chapters.title: Chapter 3: Hidden Markov Models for Regime Identification

lessons.title: Transition Matrices and Emission Distributions on Nifty Returns

body.text: A transition matrix is a map of how a regime is allowed to evolve. An emission distribution is a description of what each regime sounds like in the data. Together they turn 'which regime are we in' from a guess into an arithmetic problem.

children.text: Lesson 1 introduced a 2-state model, calm and stressed, mainly to keep the first pass simple. A 2-state transition matrix hides most of its structure, because with only two states, the off-diagonal entries are fully determined by the diagonal ones. This lesson adds a third state, elevated, sitting between calm and stressed, purely to make the transition matrix worth actually reading. Lesson 5 covers how to choose the number of states formally; for now, three is simply the smallest number that shows you something interesting.

body.caption: An illustrative 3-state transition matrix (rows: from, columns: to)

children.text: Read the matrix row by row. From Calm, the model expects to still be in Calm tomorrow 95% of the time, step up to Elevated 4% of the time, and jump straight to Stressed only 1% of the time. Now look at the Stressed row: only a 2% chance of jumping directly back to Calm tomorrow, against a 28% chance of stepping down to Elevated first. That asymmetry is not an accident of these particular numbers, it reflects a real, well-documented pattern in volatility, regimes tend to decay in stages rather than vanish overnight. A rule-based flag from Chapter 2 has no way to express that at all; it can only say 'stressed' or 'not stressed' on any given day.
Emission Distributions: What Each State 'Sounds Like'
Extend Lesson 1's calm and stressed emission parameters with a matching elevated state, keeping the annualized volatility figures roughly aligned with the India VIX bands from Chapter 2.

body.caption: Illustrative Gaussian emission parameters for all three states

children.text: In Chapter 2's toy Bayesian update, the likelihood of a -2.5% return was a hand-picked number: 0.02 under calm, 0.15 under stressed. A real emission distribution replaces that guess with an actual probability density, computed from a proper Gaussian.

body.code:
from scipy.stats import norm

calm_mean, calm_std = 0.06, 0.75
stressed_mean, stressed_std = -0.15, 2.20

todays_return = -2.5

f_calm = norm.pdf(todays_return, loc=calm_mean, scale=calm_std)
f_stressed = norm.pdf(todays_return, loc=stressed_mean, scale=stressed_std)

print(f'Calm emission density:     {f_calm:.5f}')
print(f'Stressed emission density: {f_stressed:.5f}')
print(f'Likelihood ratio (stressed / calm): {f_stressed / f_calm:.1f}x')
body.caption: Computing real emission densities for a -2.5% return under the calm and stressed Gaussians

children.text: This produces a calm density of about 0.0016 and a stressed density of about 0.1025, a likelihood ratio of roughly 65x in favor of the stressed state. These are probability densities, not probabilities on their own, a Gaussian density can exceed 1 for a narrow enough distribution, which is exactly why the next step normalizes them through Bayes' rule rather than reading them directly as probabilities.

body.code:
prior_calm, prior_stressed = 0.75, 0.25

unnormalized_calm = f_calm * prior_calm
unnormalized_stressed = f_stressed * prior_stressed
total = unnormalized_calm + unnormalized_stressed

posterior_calm = unnormalized_calm / total
posterior_stressed = unnormalized_stressed / total

print(f"P(calm | today's return):     {posterior_calm:.1%}")
print(f"P(stressed | today's return): {posterior_stressed:.1%}")
body.caption: Turning the real emission densities into a posterior belief, exactly as in Chapter 2's toy example, but with fitted numbers instead of guesses
Chapter 2's toy numbers vs this lesson's real Gaussian emissions, same -2.5% observation

body.text: The real emission distributions are far more decisive than the toy numbers, and there is a precise reason why: a -2.5% return sits 3.41 standard deviations from the calm state's mean but only 1.07 standard deviations from the stressed state's mean. Gaussian density falls off as the square of the distance in the exponent, so being roughly three times further out in standard deviation terms costs calm far more than a proportional 3x penalty, it costs it a roughly 65x one. Fitted emission distributions do not just replace a guess with a slightly better guess; they can produce dramatically sharper evidence than a hand-picked likelihood ever would.

children.text: Gaussian emissions are the standard starting choice, and also a known simplification. Real daily equity returns, Nifty included, tend to have fatter tails than a normal distribution predicts: genuinely extreme moves happen more often than a Gaussian suggests, especially clustered within the stressed state itself. Two common upgrades are worth knowing by name, even though this course sticks with Gaussian emissions for tractability: a Student's t-distribution, which has heavier tails, or a mixture of Gaussians per state, which better captures skew. Python's hmmlearn library, used in the next lesson, supports Gaussian emissions natively and can be extended to mixtures.

body.text: A Gaussian-emission HMM will systematically underestimate the probability of a genuinely extreme move, even within its own stressed state, because real crisis-day returns have fatter tails than any Gaussian, however wide. Never treat a Gaussian HMM's tail probabilities as a reliable estimate of true extreme-event risk. Chapter 8's risk management builds in safeguards for exactly this gap.

body.title: The Peak of a Gaussian Emission
body.prompt: Using the calm state's emission distribution (mean 0.06%, std dev 0.75%), what is the probability density at a return of exactly 0.06%, the mean itself? Use f(x) = 1 / (sigma * sqrt(2*pi)) at the mean, since z = 0 there.
body.explanation: At the mean, z = 0, so the density simplifies to 1 / (sigma * sqrt(2*pi)) = 1 / (0.75 × 2.5066) ≈ 0.532. This is the highest density value the calm state's Gaussian ever reaches; density falls off on both sides as the return moves away from 0.06%.

body.title: Reading the Stressed Row
body.question: According to the transition matrix in this lesson, from the Stressed state, is the model more likely to transition directly to Calm, or to step down to Elevated first?
options: Directly to Calm; volatility regimes typically resolve without an intermediate step
To Elevated first; the matrix assigns a much higher probability to stepping down through Elevated than jumping straight to Calm
Both are equally likely, since the matrix is symmetric
Neither; Stressed has the highest self-transition probability of any state, so it almost never leaves
body.explanation: The Stressed row assigns only 0.02 to a direct jump to Calm, versus 0.28 to stepping down to Elevated first, a 14-fold difference. The last option is also factually wrong on its own terms: Calm's self-transition probability (0.95) is actually higher than Stressed's (0.70) in this matrix, so Stressed is not the most persistent state here.

points: A transition matrix's off-diagonal structure only becomes informative with three or more states; a 2-state matrix's off-diagonal is fully determined by its diagonal
This lesson's illustrative matrix shows regimes decay in stages: Stressed steps down to Elevated far more often than it jumps directly back to Calm
Emission distributions turn a hand-picked likelihood into an actual computed probability density, using each state's fitted mean and standard deviation

Real Gaussian emission densities can produce far sharper posterior updates than hand-picked likelihoods, roughly 95.6% versus Chapter 2's toy 65.2%, because Gaussian density falls off extremely fast with distance from the mean

Gaussian emissions are a tractable simplification, not a perfect fit; real returns have fatter tails, which means Gaussian-based tail probabilities should never be trusted as true extreme-event risk estimates
